title: Home life
hook: he mended his own sandals, patched his clothes, and helped at home (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aisha's necklace, and a rumor that should have stopped. Your line was don't carry the rumor. Did a story reach you, and stop there? Day two hundred seventy.

For days now we've been with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in big moments: battles, treaties, sieges, revelations. It's easy to imagine a man who only ever stood in front of crowds. So somebody once asked Aisha the most ordinary question you could ask about him. What did he do at home? Not in the mosque. Not on the battlefield. At home, with the door shut, when nobody important was watching. It's a good question to ask about anyone. People can be quite different in their own kitchens. Her answer is short, and Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it. Today: home life.
screen: `BATTLES, TREATIES, CROWDS.` → `WHAT DID HE DO AT HOME?` → `AISHA ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: In Sahih al-Bukhari, Aisha says: he used to be busy serving his family, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray. Serving his family. The leader of a whole community, at home, helping. Other reports fill in the picture. Asked again, she said he mended his own sandals, patched his own clothes, milked his goat, and did the kinds of work that men do in their homes. He served himself. He didn't wait for someone to fix things for him. And home itself was simple. His rooms were small, built against the wall of the mosque, with ceilings low enough to touch. His bed, Bukhari says, was leather stuffed with palm fiber. Once Umar came in and saw the marks the rough mat had pressed into the Prophet's side, and he wept, thinking of the emperors of Persia and Rome in their luxury. The Prophet answered him gently: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we have the next? Aisha also remembered months when no fire was lit in their houses for cooking: they lived on dates and water. None of this was a show. It was just how he lived. And he put it into words in a hadith in at-Tirmidhi: the best of you are the best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family. Teachers often draw a quiet standard from it: whatever someone is in public, the measure is taken at home, with the sandals and the patches and the dishes.
screen: `BUSY SERVING HIS FAMILY.` · `SANDALS, PATCHES, THE GOAT.` · `A MAT THAT MARKED HIS SIDE.` · `THE BEST TO THEIR FAMILIES.` · then, large: `HE MENDED HIS OWN SHOES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one chore you usually skip. Sit, and picture your home. What's the task you always leave for someone else, or for later? The shoes by the door. The button that fell off. The dishes someone else usually does. The trash nobody wants to take out. Pick one. Picture yourself doing it, carefully, as if it matters, because in this story it does. If you live alone, pick the one you avoid the most. The bell holds the time.
Home life. The Prophet at home: serving his family, mending his own sandals and clothes, and living simply. Today's word.
Your line: he mended his own shoes. Today, do that one skipped chore, and don't announce it. Day two hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often hold up the Prophet's home life as a model for husbands and fathers sharing housework, often quoting Aisha's answer and the hadith that the best of you are the best to their families.

original.note: Arabic: in the service of his family, Aisha's words in Bukhari 676.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophet was above chores.
what it means: at home he served his family, mended his own sandals and clothes, and lived on very little.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 676 has fi mihnati ahlihi, in the work of his household; the sandal and patching details come in Ahmad and al-Adab al-Mufrad.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 676 (in the service of his family)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the superlative 'one of the most loved descriptions'; 'silk' (not in Bukhari 4913) became 'luxury'; the closing standard is now what teachers draw, not what 'Muslims hear' or a claim about the listener.
Hadith numbers (especially Ahmad 24903 and Adab al-Mufrad) cited from memory; confirm.
'Ceilings low enough to touch' follows a report of al-Hasan al-Basri (in Ibn Sa'd / al-Adab al-Mufrad); confirm.
Umar's weeping (Bukhari 4913) mentions Chosroes and Caesar; the script says 'kings of Persia and Rome'. Confirm.
